\chapter{Water, Wine, and Bread}
\label{ch:spanish-water-wine-bread}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name water, wine and bread in Spanish and say why a compañero is someone who shares bread with me.}

Say el agua, el vino and el pan, then open compañero into com- plus pānis and follow the root out to panadería and panadero.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el agua]{el agua — water, and an article that is not what it looks like}

\label{lesson:ES-C26-agua}



\begin{quote}
One of the least changed words in Spanish, carrying one of its most misunderstood rules. The \textquotedblleft{}masculine\textquotedblright{} article on this feminine noun is not a mistake and not an exception to gender.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{agua} (\textquotedblleft{}water\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{aqua} — almost unchanged in two thousand years. Compare French, where the \emph{very same word} was worn all the way down to a bare \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}eau,\textquotedblright{}} just the sound \textquotedblleft{}oh.\textquotedblright{} Same starting point, same span of time, wildly different amounts of erosion: how fast a language wears its words down is not fixed.

English kept the whole Latin word too, but as a \textbf{learned borrowing} rather than an inherited everyday one: \textbf{aquatic, aquarium, aqueduct, aqualung}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: el agua's article and gender}]
Notice: \textbf{el agua}, not \emph{la agua} — yet \emph{agua} is genuinely \textbf{feminine}. You can prove it: \emph{el agua \textbf{fría}, \textquotedblleft{}the cold water,\textquotedblright{} keeps the feminine adjective ending, and the plural is }las aguas\emph{, never }los aguas\emph{.}

The rule is \textbf{phonological}, not grammatical. Spanish swaps \emph{la} for \emph{el} directly before a \textbf{singular} feminine noun beginning with a \textbf{stressed \emph{a}-sound}, to avoid running two identical vowels together (\emph{la agua}). It is the same instinct that makes English pick \textquotedblleft{}an apple\textquotedblright{} over \textquotedblleft{}a apple.\textquotedblright{}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{singular} & \textbf{plural} \\
\midrule
the water & \textbf{el} agua & \textbf{las} aguas \\
the eagle & \textbf{el} águila & \textbf{las} águilas \\
the axe & \textbf{el} hacha & \textbf{las} hachas \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Only the article changes. The noun's gender never moves.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el agua\textquotedblright{} — water, feminine, but takes \emph{el}
  \item the proof — \textquotedblleft{}el agua fría\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}las aguas\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}agua\textquotedblright{} barely changed; French's \textquotedblleft{}eau\textquotedblright{} wore all the way down
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{agua} masculine or feminine? (\textbf{Feminine} — \emph{el} replaces \emph{la} only because \emph{agua} begins with a \textbf{stressed a}.) How would you prove it? (\emph{El agua \textbf{fría}}; \emph{las aguas}.) How does Spanish's erosion of \emph{aqua} compare with French's? (\textbf{Much less} — Spanish kept nearly the whole word; French wore it to \textquotedblleft{}eau.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el vino]{el vino — one word, three separate arrivals in English}

\label{lesson:ES-C26-vino}



\begin{quote}
The second drink is grammatically boring — plain masculine, plain \emph{el vino}, no stressed-\emph{a} trick. Its history makes up for that.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vino} (\textquotedblleft{}wine\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{vīnum} — which held its shape well, as French's \emph{vin} did too.

English shares the very same root by \textbf{more than one road}, and the roads are worth separating, because they show three different ways a word can travel:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English word} & \textbf{how it got there} \\
\midrule
\textbf{wine} & \emph{vīnum} borrowed \textbf{directly} into old Germanic, very early \\
\textbf{vine}, \textbf{vinegar} & borrowed centuries later, \textbf{secondhand via French} (\emph{vin + aigre}, \textquotedblleft{}sour wine\textquotedblright{}) \\
\textbf{vineyard} & \textbf{not borrowed at all} — English built it at home from the already-borrowed \emph{wine} plus native \emph{yard} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{wine} and \emph{vine} are the same Latin word twice, arriving a thousand years apart by different routes, and \emph{vineyard} is a homemade compound made out of the first arrival. One Latin noun; three English histories.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el agua, el vino\textquotedblright{} — the two drinks
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vino\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}wine, vine, vinegar\textquotedblright{} — one root, three roads
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word gives \emph{vino}? (\textbf{Vīnum}.) Name three English cousins and say how each arrived. (\textbf{Wine} — direct, early, into Germanic; \textbf{vine/vinegar} — later, via French; \textbf{vineyard} — built at home from \emph{wine} plus \emph{yard}.) And why is it \emph{el agua} but \emph{las aguas}? (The \emph{el} is a sound rule for a stressed \emph{a}, singular only.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el pan]{el pan — bread, and the friend who shares it}

\label{lesson:ES-C26-pan}



\begin{quote}
Spanish's word for bread hides the same lovely word-story you'd find in English's \textquotedblleft{}companion\textquotedblright{} — except Spanish kept \textbf{both halves}, the bread and the friendship.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pan} (\textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{pānis}. Masculine: \emph{el pan}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The Latin root \textbf{pān-} (\textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{}) gives Spanish its own word for a close friend:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{compañero / compañera} (\textquotedblleft{}companion, friend, partner\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ \emph{com-} (\textquotedblleft{}with\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{pānis} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{one you share bread with}.\textquotedblright{} Spanish built this word from the very same recipe as English \textbf{companion} and \textbf{company} (which come from the identical Latin pieces) — but where English only kept the \emph{friendship} sense, Spanish still visibly uses the \textbf{same root} for the actual \textbf{bread} (\emph{pan}) too.
  \item \textbf{panadería} (\textquotedblleft{}bakery\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{panadero} (\textquotedblleft{}baker\textquotedblright{}) — both transparently built on \emph{pan}.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{pan} and \emph{compañero} are the same word-family doing double duty in Spanish: name the food, and name the friend you'd share it with.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el pan\textquotedblright{} — bread
  \item \textquotedblleft{}compañero\textquotedblright{} — literally, one you share bread with
  \item \textquotedblleft{}panadería, panadero\textquotedblright{} — bakery, baker
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{} with its article. (\textbf{El pan}.) What does \emph{compañero} literally mean, and what's it built from? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{One you share bread with}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{com-} + \emph{pānis}.) Does English keep this same double meaning? (\textbf{No} — English's \emph{companion} only kept the friendship sense; Spanish still uses the same root for the actual bread, \emph{pan}, too.)
\end{tcolorbox}
